lessons.title: Welcome to JavaScript
lessons.description: Your first steps into the world of web programming

theorySlides.title: What is JavaScript? 🌐
theorySlides.content:
JavaScript is the programming language of the web! It makes websites interactive and dynamic.

Every website you visit uses JavaScript:
• Animations and effects
• Form validation
• Interactive maps
• Games and apps

It's one of the most popular languages in the world!

theorySlides.title: JavaScript Everywhere
theorySlides.content:
JavaScript started as a browser language, but now it runs everywhere!

🌐 Frontend: React, Vue, Angular
⚙️ Backend: Node.js, Express
📱 Mobile: React Native
🖥️ Desktop: Electron
🎮 Games: Phaser, Three.js

theorySlides.title: Your First JavaScript
theorySlides.content: Let's write your first JavaScript code! We use console.log() to display messages.
theorySlides.codeSnippet: console.log("Hello, World!");

questions.question: What is JavaScript primarily used for?
questions.explanation: JavaScript is the language of the web, making websites dynamic and interactive!

questions.question: Which function displays output in JavaScript?
questions.explanation: console.log() is the standard way to output messages in JavaScript.

questions.question: Where can JavaScript code run?
questions.explanation: JavaScript runs everywhere - in browsers (frontend), on servers with Node.js, and even in mobile/desktop apps!

questions.question: Which company originally created JavaScript?
questions.explanation: JavaScript was created by Brendan Eich at Netscape in 1995 in just 10 days!

lessons.title: Variables - Storing Data
lessons.description: Learn how to store and use information in JavaScript

theorySlides.title: What are Variables? 📦
theorySlides.content:
Variables are containers for storing data. Think of them as labeled boxes where you can put information.

In JavaScript, we have three ways to create variables:
• let - for values that change
• const - for values that stay the same
• var - the old way (avoid using)

theorySlides.title: Creating Variables
theorySlides.content: Here's how to create and use variables:

theorySlides.title: Data Types
theorySlides.content:
JavaScript has several data types:

📝 String: "Hello" (text in quotes)
🔢 Number: 42, 3.14 (numbers)
✅ Boolean: true, false
📋 Array: [1, 2, 3] (lists)
📦 Object: {name: "Alex"} (complex data)

questions.question: Which keyword creates a variable that cannot be changed?
questions.explanation: const creates constants - values that cannot be reassigned.

questions.question: What type is the value "Hello"?
questions.explanation: Text in quotes is called a String in JavaScript.

questions.question: What happens if you use a variable before declaring it with let?
questions.explanation: With let, variables are not hoisted like var. Accessing them before declaration causes a ReferenceError (temporal dead zone).

questions.question: Which statement about const is true?
options: The value can never be modified
questions.explanation: const prevents reassignment of the variable, but if it's an object or array, the contents can still be modified!

questions.question: What is the result of: typeof null?
questions.explanation: This is a famous JavaScript quirk! typeof null returns "object" - a bug that can't be fixed due to backward compatibility.

lessons.title: Operators - Math & Logic
lessons.description: Learn to perform calculations and comparisons

theorySlides.title: Math Operators ➕
theorySlides.content:
JavaScript can do math! Here are the basic operators:

+ Addition
- Subtraction
* Multiplication
/ Division
% Modulus (remainder)
** Exponentiation (power)

theorySlides.title: Math Examples
theorySlides.content: Let's see operators in action:
theorySlides.codeSnippet:
let sum = 10 + 5;      // 15
let diff = 10 - 3;     // 7
let product = 4 * 3;   // 12
let quotient = 15 / 3; // 5
let remainder = 17 % 5; // 2
let power = 2 ** 3;    // 8

theorySlides.title: Comparison Operators
theorySlides.content:
Compare values to get true or false:

== Equal value
=== Equal value AND type
!= Not equal
> Greater than
< Less than
>= Greater or equal
<= Less or equal
theorySlides.codeSnippet:
console.log(5 > 3);   // true
console.log(10 === 10); // true
console.log(5 !== 3);  // true

questions.question: What is 17 % 5?
questions.explanation: The modulus operator returns the remainder. 17 ÷ 5 = 3 remainder 2.

questions.question: What does === check?
questions.explanation: === checks both value AND type. "5" === 5 is false!

questions.question: What is the result of: 5 + "5"?
questions.explanation: JavaScript coerces the number to a string and concatenates them, resulting in "55". This is type coercion in action!

questions.question: Which operator would you use to check if two values are NOT equal in type AND value?
questions.explanation: !== is the strict inequality operator. It returns true if values differ in value OR type.

theorySlides.title: Strings - Text Data 📝
theorySlides.content:
Strings are text values. You can create them with:

• Single quotes: 'Hello'
• Double quotes: "Hello"
• Backticks: `Hello` (template literals)

Backticks are special - they allow embedding variables!

theorySlides.title: Template Literals
theorySlides.content: Template literals let you embed expressions:

theorySlides.title: String Methods
theorySlides.content:
Strings have useful methods:

.length - get length
.toUpperCase() - UPPERCASE
.toLowerCase() - lowercase
.includes() - check if contains
.slice() - extract part
theorySlides.codeSnippet:
let text = "JavaScript";
console.log(text.length);      // 10
console.log(text.toUpperCase()); // JAVASCRIPT
console.log(text.includes("Script")); // true

questions.question: Which quotes allow embedding variables?
questions.explanation: Only backticks (template literals) allow ${variable} syntax.

questions.question: What does "hello".toUpperCase() return?
questions.explanation: toUpperCase() converts all letters to uppercase.

questions.question: What is the output of: `The answer is 8`?
questions.explanation: Template literals (backticks) evaluate expressions inside ${}. So 5 + 3 becomes 8.

questions.question: How do you get the length of a string "hello"?
questions.explanation: .length is a property (not a method), so no parentheses are needed. "hello".length returns 5.

questions.question: What does "JavaScript".slice(0, 4) return?
questions.explanation: slice(0, 4) extracts characters from index 0 to 3 (end index is exclusive), returning "Java".

lessons.title: If Statements - Making Decisions
lessons.description: Learn to write code that makes choices

theorySlides.title: Conditional Logic 🤔
theorySlides.content:
Programs need to make decisions! If statements let your code choose different paths based on conditions.

Think of it like: "IF it's raining, THEN take umbrella, ELSE wear sunglasses"

theorySlides.title: If Statement Syntax
theorySlides.content: Here's how to write if statements:

theorySlides.title: Multiple Conditions
theorySlides.content: Use else if for multiple conditions:

questions.question: What does the else block do?
questions.explanation: The else block executes when the if condition is false.

questions.question: If x = 5, what does (x > 3) evaluate to?
questions.explanation: 5 is greater than 3, so the condition is true.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the else if statement?
options: To run code when all conditions are false
questions.explanation: else if allows you to test multiple conditions in order. The first true condition executes, then the rest are skipped.

questions.question: What is the result of: true && false?
questions.explanation: The && (AND) operator returns true only if BOTH operands are true. Here, false makes the whole expression false.

lessons.title: Working with Arrays
lessons.description: Master JavaScript arrays and their methods

theorySlides.title: What are Arrays? 📚
theorySlides.content:
Arrays store multiple values in a single variable. They are ordered and can hold any data type.

Common uses:
• User lists
• Shopping carts
• Playlists
• Game scores

theorySlides.title: Creating Arrays
theorySlides.content: Arrays use square brackets with comma-separated values.

theorySlides.title: Array Methods
theorySlides.content: JavaScript provides powerful array methods.

theorySlides.title: Useful Array Methods
theorySlides.content: More methods for common tasks.

questions.question: Which method adds an element to the end?
questions.explanation: push() adds elements to the end of an array.

questions.question: How do you access the first element?
questions.explanation: Arrays are zero-indexed, so arr[0] is the first element.

questions.question: What does the spread operator (...) do with arrays?
questions.explanation: The spread operator (...) expands array elements. Example: [...arr1, ...arr2] combines two arrays.

questions.question: What is array destructuring?
questions.explanation: Destructuring unpacks array values: const [a, b] = [1, 2] assigns a=1, b=2. It's a clean way to extract values!

questions.question: What does [1,2,3].filter(n => n > 1) return?
questions.explanation: filter() creates a new array with elements that pass the test. Only 2 and 3 are greater than 1.

questions.question: What is the key difference between for...of and for...in?
options: for...of iterates values, for...in iterates keys
for...in iterates values, for...of iterates keys

questions.question: How do you exit a loop early?

theorySlides.title: What are Objects? 🏷️
theorySlides.content:
Objects store data as key-value pairs (properties). They represent real-world entities.

Examples:
• User profiles
• Product details
• Game characters
• Configuration settings

theorySlides.title: Creating Objects
theorySlides.content: Objects use curly braces with property: value pairs.

theorySlides.title: Object Methods
theorySlides.content: Objects can contain functions (methods).

theorySlides.title: Object Manipulation
theorySlides.content: Add, update, or delete properties dynamically.

questions.question: How do you access object properties?
questions.explanation: Use dot notation or bracket notation to access properties.

questions.question: What is "this" in an object method?
questions.explanation: "this" refers to the object the method belongs to.

questions.question: What is object destructuring?
questions.explanation: Destructuring extracts properties: const {name, age} = person assigns person.name to name and person.age to age.

questions.question: What does Object.keys(obj) return?
questions.explanation: Object.keys() returns an array of an object's property names (keys). Object.values() returns the values.

questions.question: How do you create a shallow copy of an object?
questions.explanation: The spread operator {...obj} creates a shallow copy. Alternatively, use Object.assign({}, obj).

questions.question: What is the syntax for arrow functions?

questions.question: What does the map() method do?

questions.question: What is a closure in JavaScript?
options: A way to close a function
A function with access to its outer scope
questions.explanation: A closure is when a function "remembers" variables from its outer scope, even after that scope has finished executing!

questions.question: What is the difference between function declarations and arrow functions regarding "this"?

questions.question: What does the reduce() method do?

questions.explanation: reduce() executes a reducer function on each element, resulting in a single output value. Example: sum all numbers.

lessons.title: Asynchronous JavaScript
lessons.description: Handle timing, promises, and async operations

theorySlides.title: What is Async? ⏱️
theorySlides.content:
Asynchronous code doesn't wait for operations to complete. It continues running and handles results later.

Common async operations:
• Network requests
• File reading
• Database queries
• Timers

theorySlides.title: Callbacks
theorySlides.content: The original way to handle async operations.

theorySlides.title: Promises
theorySlides.content: Modern way to handle async operations. A promise represents a future value.

theorySlides.title: Async/Await
theorySlides.content: The cleanest syntax for async code. Makes it read like synchronous code.

questions.question: What does setTimeout() do?
questions.explanation: setTimeout() delays code execution by a specified time.

questions.question: What keyword makes a function async?
questions.explanation: The async keyword makes a function asynchronous.

questions.question: What does await do?
questions.explanation: await pauses async function execution until the promise resolves, making async code look synchronous. Only works inside async functions!

questions.question: What are the three states of a Promise?
questions.explanation: A Promise can be pending (initial), fulfilled (successful), or rejected (failed). Use .then() for fulfilled and .catch() for rejected.

questions.question: What is Promise.all() used for?
options: Running promises one at a time
questions.explanation: Promise.all() runs multiple promises concurrently and resolves when ALL complete (or rejects if ANY fails). Great for parallel operations!
